title: Not by breath
theme: No mortal lives by out-breath or in-breath, but by another on whom both depend.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «मनुष्यो देहवान्», an embodied human being
Śaṅkara: by one different from the assembled breaths, «इतरेणैव संहतप्राणादिविलक्षणेन»

words.role: verb of the second half-line; the subject is all beings

words.context: the two breaths, prāṇa and apāna

words.gram: past passive participle, m. nom. du.

sandhi.rule: Two like vowels merge into the long vowel, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).
-aḥ becomes -o before a voiced consonant, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च).
A final n after a short vowel is doubled before a vowel, P. 8.3.32 (ङमो ह्रस्वादचि ङमुण्नित्यम्).
au becomes āv before a vowel, P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः).

morphology.note: kaḥ, ‘who’, with the particle cana, ‘any(one) at all’; with the negative na, ‘no one’. The visarga becomes ś before c.
upa-ā-√śri, ‘lean on, rest on’, past participle in the dual: the two breaths rest on the one by whom all live.

translation.literal: Not by the out-breath, not by the in-breath does any mortal live; but they live by another, on whom these two rest.
translation.readable: No mortal lives by the out-breath or the in-breath. All live by something else, on which these two breaths themselves depend.

anvaya: कश्चन मर्त्यः न प्राणेन न अपानेन जीवति । [सर्वे] तु इतरेण जीवन्ति यस्मिन् एतौ उपाश्रितौ ।
syntax: Two contrasting clauses: a double negative (na … na …) with the singular jīvati, then the plural jīvanti with the instrumental itareṇa; the relative clause yasmin etau upāśritau describes this ‘other’.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the self, unlike the breaths an unassembled being, for whose sake the assembled breaths work, as a house is for its dweller, «यथा गृहादीनां लोके». Raṅgarāmānuja: the supreme Self, on whom even the life of the breaths depends, «यदधीनं प्राणापानयोरपि जीवनम् तदधीनमेव सर्वेषां जीवनमिति भावः». Madhva: Viṣṇu, on whom breath rests to sustain beings.

beginner: We usually say that breathing keeps us alive. The verse disagrees: no one lives by the breath going out or the breath coming in. We live by something else, on which the breathing itself depends. Śaṅkara argues it like this: the breaths and senses are parts that work together, and things that are put together work for someone other than themselves, as a house is built for the person who lives in it. So the breaths cannot be the final reason we are alive. Raṅgarāmānuja says the whole life of every being depends on the supreme Self, who even keeps the breath going. Madhva says breath can carry living beings only because it rests on Viṣṇu.
analogy: Like a pair of oars that move the boat, though neither oar is the rower who pulls them.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: No mortal lives by out-breath or in-breath; all live by another, on whom those two rest.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The breaths cannot be the cause of life, because what is assembled works for another, «न ह्येषां परार्थानां संहत्यकारित्वाज्जीवनहेतुत्वमुपपद्यते», as houses do in the world, «यथा गृहादीनां लोके». We live by another, different from the assembled breaths, «इतरेणैव संहतप्राणादिविलक्षणेन», in whose presence and for whose sake they act.

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: the life of all depends on him
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The verse states the greatness of the Supreme as the cause of the breathing of every being, «तस्य सर्वप्राणिप्राणनहेतुत्वरूपं महिमानमाह». On him the life of the two breaths depends, and so the life of all, «यदधीनं प्राणापानयोरपि जीवनम् तदधीनमेव सर्वेषां जीवनमिति भावः».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: His bhāṣya comments once on 2.2.3–5, in a verse that names no source: breath alone does not sustain conscious beings, «न केवलं प्राण एव चेतनानां विधारकः», but sustains them by resting on Viṣṇu, «किन्तु विष्णुं समाश्रित्य प्राणो जीवान् बिभर्त्ययम्», who is their chief and independent support.

advaita.text: Life is from the self, other than the assembled breaths, «इतरेणैव संहतप्राणादिविलक्षणेन».

visistadvaita.text: The supreme Self causes the breathing of all beings, «तस्य सर्वप्राणिप्राणनहेतुत्वरूपं महिमानमाह».

dvaita.text: Viṣṇu is the chief and independent support of conscious beings, «अतो मुख्याश्रयो विष्णुश्चेतनानां स्वतन्त्रतः».

schools.disagreement: All three read the ‘other’ as that on which breath depends: the self, unlike any assembled thing (Śaṅkara); the supreme Self who causes all breathing (Raṅgarāmānuja); Viṣṇu, on whom breath rests (Madhva).

parallels.quote: यत्प्राणेन न प्राणिति येन प्राणः प्रणीयते
parallels.note: The Kena makes the same point: Brahman is that by which breath is led, not what breathes by breath.
The Taittirīya asks who would breathe in or out if that bliss were not; breathing depends on something beyond it.

contemporary.text: A body can be kept breathing by a machine, and we still ask whether someone is there. The verse locates life not in the mechanics of breathing but in that for which the breathing goes on. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: If you are not your breath, what are you?
reflect.deeper: Is Śaṅkara’s argument from assembled things convincing to you? What would it take to refute it?
reflect.practice: Watch three breaths and notice the one who is watching them.

flags.note: The ‘other’: the self (Śaṅkara), the supreme Self (Raṅgarāmānuja) or Viṣṇu (Madhva).
madhva.json files one comment under 2.2.3, 2.2.4 and 2.2.5; it closes ॥ ३५ ॥ (a running number, not ours) and concerns breath upheld by Viṣṇu, which bears on this verse; it is quoted here only.
